infant-peekaboo.title: Share a game of peekaboo
infant-peekaboo.invitation: Share the surprise of peekaboo, then pause for their reply.
infant-peekaboo.summary: Play a little peekaboo together, leaving time for your baby’s look, sound, or gesture in reply.
infant-peekaboo.cue: Your baby is interested when someone disappears briefly and comes back.
detail: The authors include peekaboo among the games in their 9–12-month language section. Enjoy the back-and-forth and follow the response your baby gives.
A look, a movement, or a sound can be part of the exchange. There is no word your baby has to say to take part.

baby-language.title: A conversation with your baby
baby-language.invitation: Answer their sound, then leave a little room for the reply.
baby-language.summary: Answer a sound, smile or gesture, then pause. Your baby’s next response can guide the conversation.
baby-language.cue: Your baby is watching your face or experimenting with sounds.
detail: Come where your baby can see your face. Say something, listen, and leave a little space for their sound or movement. You can echo a sound, smile back, or put a few words to what seems to interest them.
Raspberries, bubbles and changes in volume are part of the vocal play the authors describe. There is no need to ask for a particular sound or word.

For families who choose baby signs, the book suggests pairing a few familiar spoken words with signs, such as “milk” or “done.” Its age labels differ between sections; the authors’ wider guidance is to notice the baby’s response and interest.

baby-connection.title: Let them know before a pickup
baby-connection.invitation: When a pickup can wait, let them know and pause for their response.
baby-connection.summary: When a pickup can wait, come into view, say what you have in mind, and pause for a response. Necessary care or protection still calls for gentle action.
baby-connection.cue: You are about to pick your baby up, and there is time to make it an exchange.
detail: Come where your baby can see you and let them know you would like to pick them up. Wait and notice their expression or movement. If they turn away and the pickup can wait, give them more time.
Their response is something to listen to, not a certain yes-or-no signal. When care, comfort or protection is needed, the authors describe telling the baby what is happening and acting gently.
